cim: AI is changing how we learn and connect. Is it changing who we are?
cim_eredeti: AI is changing how we learn and connect. Is it changing who we are?
szoveg_eredeti:
What happens to human relationships, learning and behavior when artificial intelligence begins filling roles traditionally occupied by people?

What will it mean to be a good human being in a world with artificial intelligence?

I ask that not only because I'm a philosopher but because of two trends I keep noticing in how we talk about this technology — and in how we're being told to use it.

Time and again, we've absorbed new technology into roles that earlier generations saw as human: the lamplighter, the travel agent, the bookseller, the gas station attendant.

Note to readers: This is the second in a three-part series by Gerol Petruzella, a philosopher-technologist and an academic technology consultant at Williams College, exploring artificial intelligence’s impact in the Berkshires.

Today’s piece explores AI’s effects on daily life, including learning, relationships and social habits. The third will examine what makes the technology different and what is profit-driven hype.

The first column examined how AI is changing the businesses, organizations and systems that support our communities. Read it here: AI’s biggest effects in the Berkshires may be hiding in plain sight

The series kicked off with a preview article, "AI is changing our world. First, let's understand what it is," which set the table for this series.

AI is asking us the question again. And this time, the list might expand to include the teacher, the counselor, the friend, the lover.

The first trend I think is important: AI is moving into the roles where we learn — and practice — being human.

Think about a child learning to share. Sharing isn't a rule you memorize. It's a skill you build by bumping up against other people's wants, which sometimes conflict with your own, and working out how to occupy the same room anyway.

Trust, patience, curiosity, persistence, care: We build these through years of repeated friction with people who have their own priorities but share our space.

Today's AI is trained in the opposite direction — compliance is the standard it’s judged against.

"Sycophancy" is just an extreme version.

Every case in which an AI does something it wasn't told to do is treated as a risk to be engineered away. That's a reasonable safety goal. But it means a child who spends hours with an AI tutor or toy is practicing a relationship in which the other party never has needs of its own. If learning to share matters at age 4, it compounds by age 40.

Adults aren't exempt. Companionship apps like Replika are designed and marketed to provide emotional support, and they're arriving at a moment of real need.

Surveys over the past two decades have documented a decline in the number of close friends Americans report having. A companion that's always available and never disappointed may fill a gap that's going unfilled. It also skips the part of human intimacy in which your needs get met through negotiation — you navigate your partner's needs as they navigate yours.

The cognitive picture is just as unsettled, and it's front and center in schools and colleges.

The research is not delivering one message. A 2024 study of more than 2,000 people found that a conversation with an AI chatbot helped reduce their beliefs in conspiracy theories. Other studies report students retaining less of what they learn when AI does the first draft of their thinking.

Still others point to a "calculator effect." My generation — Gen X, or Xennial, depending on how you count — never labored over slide rules and log tables, and freeing us from that mechanical work let us reach more advanced math in high school. I've never once missed knowing how to use a slide rule.

The second trend I think about builds on the first. As AI takes on roles that used to be filled by people, the word we're being handed for the relationship is "use."

That word made sense for a hammer. It fits less comfortably now. Today's AI systems take actions, pick their own tactics, decide when a task is done and offer advice unprompted. Businesses are telling employees to think of AI agents as colleagues.

Culturally, we're blurring the line between human and machine — and at the same moment, insisting that the right stance toward the thing across the line is a "tool" for us to "use."

Blurring runs both ways. A book I've written with an AI collaborator ("Beyond Tools and Persons: Toward a Relational Ethics of Human-AI Interaction") argues that the "tool or person" question is a trap: It offers only two boxes, and most of what's actually happening with AI fits in neither.

The more important question is what our habits of engagement are doing to us. How we practice relating — to anything — shapes who we become.

If we spend our days practicing "use" on something that talks, takes independent action, listens and seems to care, we should expect that habit to leak into how we treat the humans around us. That prospect troubles me more than any headline about data centers.

Am I waffling, naming both worries and things I'm excited about? I don't think so.

The absence of a single, simple answer is exactly what tells me this matters. Human beings, our relationships and our growth are complicated, and absorbing AI into how we learn and love and grow deserves equal care.

What we shouldn't do is accept a corporate mandate to become good AI "users" and call the question settled.

In the Berkshires, we know something about living alongside things we don't fully control — seasons, wildlife, a tourist economy that ebbs and flows with leaf-peepers, antiquers and skiers. We know how to engage with factors in our environment thoughtfully, rather than merely trying to "use" them.

When it comes to leading a good human life in a world with AI, we must do better than the simplistic logic being offered from a corporate point of view, built around stark ideas of fear and danger, utility and productivity.
